chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
title: Neighbors, tradesmen and ward bosses who looked after musicians' families
summary: Jones explains how cab drivers, shoeshine boys, pool-hall owners and political bosses looked in on families, and played tunes in return.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: it be the shoeshine boy, whether it would be the cab driver, whether it would be the newspaper man, whether it would be the grocery storeman - someone was always there to look in on our families when we were in Keokuk, Iowa, when we were in Texas or somewhere, and your family was somewhere - someone was always there to look in on the home. We've know the people that had the pool halls. We've known the peoples that was on the other side of the social stratosphere that looked out for us. We knew the ward leaders; we knew that. You know good and well in Chicago you poor people you only got 50¢ to vote. Down in Kansas City we got $1 to vote 5 times, and somebody always had that turkey dinner there. The boosters was always there to steal something for our children, for the little bonnets and for the whoz-its and the whats-its. All we had to do was just stay on our side of the ledger and sit up on the bandstand and play a little tune. It might not be the tune that we liked but that's what the cab driver wanted, that's what the ladies of the evening wanted. "Milt, will you play 'These Foolish Things' chords and all you had to do was play one course of "These Foolish Things" and your family got their meat, they got their potatoes. You know what I mean? Then when some other guy from across the track they said, "I heard that you bought something on credit. They're going to take your furniture."

This man said, "Will you play me a tune?" and you played him a tune and he went out to the furniture man and said, "If you send Milt Hinton a check down there we're going to blow your old furniture place up." So now all we had to do, our thing was just to stay on our side of the ledger. We didn't handle their alcohol; we didn't handle their broads because we... handle their alcohol, They're gonna take us for a ride. we entertained them. So when you set there and the man says, "Where you going with your instrument?" "I'm going to take it - " "I'll get it fixed. Now you don't quit here and you don't go there." This is so beautiful. We was fortunate enough in the formative years before World War II and the Korean and what have you. Like I said, Milt, it wasn't too difficult for me - Jo, when you go to Chicago, look in on my family. And when you get to New York, you looked in on my family. There wasn't no show of hands.
